plan: SAT R&W batch 58: 8 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000520..000527 (dense-text approach continued; mantis shrimp topic dropped as already banked), plus S057-04 resubmitted as revision 2 on its corrected, previously unbanked passage CLD-P-SAT-RW-000515. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Short sentences
passages.text: Some reviewers have called the novelist's prose ______, but the charge mistakes economy for poverty: her sentences are short not because she lacks resources but because every word in them has been weighed and the unnecessary ones discarded.

passages.title: Plants that stop flinching
passages.text: The leaves of Mimosa pudica fold up when the plant is disturbed, a response thought to protect it from being eaten. In one experiment, researchers repeatedly dropped potted Mimosa plants a short distance onto a padded surface. At first the plants folded their leaves after each drop, but after many drops most plants stopped folding. When the same plants were then shaken, a disturbance they had not experienced before, they folded their leaves at once. This result suggests that the plants' failure to fold after repeated drops was not simply ______

passages.title: The stability of print
passages.text:
Text 1
In an influential study, historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that the printing press transformed European learning by making texts fixed. Once a work was printed, she contended, hundreds of identical copies could circulate, so that scholars in different cities could be confident they were reading the same words.

Text 2
Historian Adrian Johns points out that early printed books were often anything but reliable. Printers pirated one another's editions, introduced errors, and sometimes altered texts to suit buyers. Readers trusted a printed book, Johns argues, only when they trusted the people and institutions behind it, such as reputable printers, licensing systems, and learned societies, and that trust took generations to build.

passages.title: Parks and birds
passages.text:
An ecologist surveyed bird species in five city parks.
Park | Area (hectares) | Bird species recorded
P | 2 | 14
Q | 5 | 22
R | 9 | 19
S | 12 | 31
T | 20 | 38
The ecologist concluded that although larger parks generally had more bird species, park area alone did not determine the number of species recorded.

passages.title: Small area, many species
passages.text: Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean ______ they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species.

passages.title: A report on transit
passages.text: After two years of study, the city's transit commission released ______ final report, which recommended extending light-rail service to the airport.

passages.title: Bike lanes on Main Street
passages.text: When the city built protected bike lanes on Main Street, planners predicted that many residents who had been afraid to ride in traffic would begin commuting by bicycle. ______ bicycle traffic on the street tripled within a year, while car traffic barely changed.

passages.title: Seeing the unseen
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Inge Lehmann was a Danish seismologist.
- In 1936, she analyzed records of earthquake waves and concluded that Earth has a solid inner core.
- Marie Tharp was an American geologist and mapmaker.
- In the 1950s, she used measurements of ocean depth to map a rift valley running along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
- Neither scientist directly observed the structure she identified.

passages.title: Words for blue
passages.text:
Text 1
Some scholars have argued that the language a person speaks determines what that person can perceive: if a language lacks separate words for two colors, its speakers cannot truly see them as different.

Text 2
Russian has two basic words for blue: goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker ones. In one experiment, Russian speakers told apart two blues faster when the blues fell on opposite sides of that boundary than when both fell on the same side; English speakers, who use one basic word for both, showed no such difference. But the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they performed a verbal task, such as silently repeating a string of digits, at the same time, while a nonverbal task did not remove it. Language, the researchers concluded, can influence perception, but only while words are actively being used.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the charge mistakes economy for poverty
candidates.explanation: The reviewers' charge must suggest poverty, a lack of resources; "threadbare" means worn thin or impoverished, which the author recasts as deliberate economy.

A.rationale: "Laconic" means using few words, which is the economy the author praises, not the poverty the reviewers allege.

C.rationale: "Ornate" means elaborately decorated, the opposite of short, spare sentences.

D.rationale: "Derivative" charges imitation, but the author's reply is about scarcity versus economy, not originality.

hints: What does the author say the reviewers mistook economy for?
candidates.remember: The blank should match the charge, not the author's defense.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a response that the plants would show to any repeated disturbance.
choices.B: a sign that folding protects the plants from being eaten.
choices.C: a loss of the physical ability to fold their leaves.
choices.D: a reaction to the padded surface onto which the plants were dropped.

candidates.evidence: they folded their leaves at once
candidates.explanation: If the plants had simply worn out, they would not have folded when shaken. Because they still folded to a new disturbance, their failure to fold after drops was not fatigue; it was a change specific to the repeated drops.

A.rationale: The text tests only one repeated disturbance; the shaking result does not support a claim about every kind of repetition.

B.rationale: Protection from being eaten is the background purpose of folding, not an explanation of why folding stopped.

D.rationale: The padding is part of the method; nothing suggests it caused the plants to stop folding.

hints: What would the shaking result look like if the plants were just exhausted?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the new disturbance rules out.

candidates.remember: A control condition rules out an alternative explanation.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Johns (Text 2) most likely respond to Eisenstein's claim in Text 1 that printing made texts fixed?

choices.A: By agreeing that printing made texts fixed as soon as identical copies began to circulate
choices.B: By denying that the printing press had any important effect on how European scholars read
choices.C: By claiming that handwritten copies were more reliable than printed books ever became
choices.D: By arguing that stability came from slowly developed social practices, not the press alone

candidates.explanation: Johns does not deny printing's importance; he argues that reliability came from trusted printers, licensing, and societies over generations rather than from the technology itself.

A.rationale: Johns stresses piracy, errors, and alterations in early printed books, which contradicts immediate fixity.

B.rationale: Johns challenges how printing produced trust, not whether it mattered at all.

C.rationale: Johns never compares printed books with handwritten copies.

hints: Does Johns reject printing's importance, or the source of its stability?

strategy.explanation: Compare what each text credits for reliable texts.

candidates.remember: A response can accept an effect while disputing its cause.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the ecologist's conclusion?

choices.A: Park R was larger than park Q but had fewer bird species recorded than park Q.
choices.B: Park T, the largest park, had the most bird species recorded of all five parks.
choices.C: Park S had more than twice as many bird species recorded as park P had.
choices.D: The five parks together had a total area of 48 hectares.

candidates.evidence: park area alone did not determine the number of species recorded
candidates.explanation: The conclusion has two parts. The general trend is visible in the table, but the second part needs an exception: park R (9 hectares) had fewer species than the smaller park Q (5 hectares).

B.rationale: This supports the general trend but not the claim that area alone did not determine species numbers.

C.rationale: This fits the general trend and does not show any exception to it.

D.rationale: The total area says nothing about how area relates to species numbers.

hints: Which part of the conclusion needs an exception?

strategy.explanation: Look for a pair of parks that breaks the trend.

candidates.remember: Support a qualification with a counterexample.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "yet" need a comma before it.

A.rationale: Without a comma before "yet," the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

D.rationale: A colon introduces an explanation or example, but the second clause contrasts with the first.

hints: How many independent clauses are there?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two clauses.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The antecedent "commission" is singular and acts as one body, so the singular possessive "its" is correct.

A.rationale: "Commission" is a singular collective noun here, so the plural "their" does not agree.

B.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which does not make sense before "final report."

D.rationale: "They're" means "they are" and is also plural.

candidates.remember: A collective noun acting as one unit takes singular pronouns.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: bicycle traffic on the street tripled within a year
candidates.explanation: The second sentence confirms the planners' prediction, so a transition that adds emphasis or confirmation, "Indeed," fits.

A.rationale: The tripling of bicycle traffic confirms the prediction; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: "Instead" signals that something replaced what was expected, but the result matched the prediction.

C.rationale: "Still" signals a result in spite of something, but nothing in the first sentence works against the result.

hints: Did the result match or contradict the prediction?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the second sentence confirms or opposes the first.

candidates.remember: "Indeed" confirms or strengthens a previous point.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity in how Lehmann and Tharp made their discoveries. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Lehmann and Tharp each identified a structure no one could see directly by analyzing existing measurements.
choices.B: Lehmann, a Danish seismologist, studied Earth's interior, while Tharp, an American mapmaker, studied the ocean floor.
choices.C: In 1936, Lehmann concluded from records of earthquake waves that Earth has a solid inner core.
choices.D: In the 1950s, Tharp used ocean-depth measurements to map a rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

candidates.evidence: Neither scientist directly observed the structure she identified.
candidates.explanation: The goal is a similarity in method. Choice A says that both inferred unseen structures from existing measurements, which combines the last note with the details of both discoveries.

B.rationale: This contrasts their fields rather than showing a similarity in method.

C.rationale: This describes only Lehmann's discovery, not a similarity with Tharp's.

D.rationale: This describes only Tharp's discovery, not a similarity with Lehmann's.

hints: Which choice mentions both scientists and something they share?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for both scientists and a shared method.

candidates.remember: A similarity statement must include both subjects.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?

choices.A: They would agree, since Russian speakers saw differences between blues that English speakers could not see.
choices.B: They would reject any role for language in perception, since the Russian speakers' advantage could be removed.
choices.C: They would say that the claim is supported for color but should be tested for other kinds of perception.
choices.D: They would say that language can speed some perceptual judgments but does not fix what speakers are able to see.

candidates.evidence: only while words are actively being used
candidates.explanation: Text 2 shows a real but limited effect: Russian speakers were faster across the goluboy/siniy boundary, but only when verbal processing was available. That supports influence, not the determination Text 1 claims.

A.rationale: English speakers could still tell the blues apart; the Russian advantage was in speed across the boundary, not in what could be seen.

B.rationale: The researchers conclude that language can influence perception, though not in the way Text 1 claims.

C.rationale: The results contradict the strong claim even for color, because the effect depends on in-the-moment verbal processing.

hints: Does Text 2 show that language determines perception, or something weaker?

strategy.explanation: Compare the strength of each text's claim.

candidates.remember: Watch for responses that accept a weaker version of a claim.

revision_history.reason: solver B: passage overstated the study (category advantage, not an overall Russian-English speed difference)
revision_history.change: passage (not yet banked) reworded to describe the cross-boundary advantage; closing sentence clarified
